table.caption: Five series, each starting at $n = 1$ ($k$ is a positive constant)

p-series-s2.title: Partial sums of the harmonic series

plot.label: Partial sums of the harmonic series for n = 1 to 20, each above the dashed curve y = ln(x + 1)

p-series-s2.text: The dots are the partial sums $S_n = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}$ of the harmonic series for $n = 1$ to $20$. The dashed curve is $y = \ln(x + 1)$; by the integral test picture, $S_n \ge \ln(n + 1)$ for every $n$.

items.q: Which of the series I, II, III and IV converge?
options: I, II and IV
I, III and IV
IV alone
I and IV

why.correct: A $p$-series $\sum \frac{1}{n^p}$ converges exactly when $p > 1$. I: $p = \frac{3}{2}$. II: $p = \frac{1}{3}$. III: $\frac{n^2}{n^3} = \frac{1}{n}$, $p = 1$. IV: $p = \pi$. So I and IV converge.
options: Series II has $p = \frac{1}{3}$, which is not greater than 1.
Series III simplifies to $\frac{1}{n}$: $p = 1$, the harmonic series, which diverges.
Series I has $p = \frac{3}{2} > 1$, so it converges too.
Right: $p = \frac{3}{2}$ and $p = \pi$ are both greater than 1.

items.q: What is series III, and does it converge?
options: A $p$-series with $p = 5$; it converges
A $p$-series with $p = \frac{2}{3}$; it diverges
The harmonic series $\sum \frac{1}{n}$; it diverges
The harmonic series $\sum \frac{1}{n}$; it converges

why.correct: $\frac{n^2}{n^3} = \frac{1}{n}$: the harmonic series, the $p$-series with $p = 1$, which diverges.
options: Simplify first: the powers subtract, $\frac{n^2}{n^3} = n^{-1}$.
$\frac{n^2}{n^3}$ is not $n^{-2/3}$: subtract the exponents, $2 - 3 = -1$.
Right: $\frac{n^2}{n^3} = \frac{1}{n}$, so $p = 1$.
The harmonic series diverges, though its terms approach 0.

items.q: Series II is a $p$-series. What is $p$?

mistakes.why: A cube root is the power $\frac{1}{3}$, not 3.
$p$ is the power in the denominator: $\frac{1}{n^{1/3}}$ has $p = \frac{1}{3}$.

why.correct: $\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{n}} = \frac{1}{n^{1/3}}$, so $p = \frac{1}{3}$, and since $p \le 1$ the series diverges.

items.q: For which values of $k$ does series V converge? Give an interval.

ends.lo: At $k = \frac{1}{2}$, $2k = 1$: the harmonic series, which diverges, so $k = \frac{1}{2}$ is left out.

mistakes.why: At $k = \frac{1}{2}$ the series is $\sum \frac{1}{n}$, which diverges; the condition is $p > 1$, strictly.

why.correct: Series V is a $p$-series with $p = 2k$. It converges when $2k > 1$, that is $k > \frac{1}{2}$.

items.q: What does the graph, with $S_n \ge \ln(n + 1)$, show about the harmonic series?
options: It converges: the partial sums grow more and more slowly
It converges to about 3.6, the last partial sum shown
Nothing: the terms approach 0
It diverges: its lower bound grows without bound

why.correct: $\ln(n + 1) \to \infty$ and $S_n \ge \ln(n + 1)$, so $S_n \to \infty$: the harmonic series diverges.
options: Slowing growth is not leveling off; $S_n$ passes every number eventually.
$S_{20} \approx 3.6$, but the partial sums keep growing past it.
The nth term test is silent, but the lower bound $\ln(n + 1)$ settles it.
Right: a lower bound that grows without bound drags the partial sums up with it.

items.q: Find $S_4$, the sum of the first four terms of the harmonic series.

mistakes.why: Fractions do not add top-to-top and bottom-to-bottom; use the common denominator 12.
That is the fourth term alone; $S_4$ adds the first four terms.

items.q: Using only $S_n \ge \ln(n + 1)$, which condition on $n$ guarantees $S_n > 5$?
options: $n > 5$, so that the later terms are each below $\frac{1}{5}$

why.correct: $S_n \ge \ln(n + 1)$, so whenever $\ln(n + 1) > 5$, $S_n > 5$. That holds once $n + 1 > e^5 \approx 148.4$, so from $n = 148$ on. (The bound is cautious: the partial sums actually pass 5 at $n = 83$.)
options: A lower bound below 5 says nothing about whether $S_n$ is above 5.
Right: if the lower bound passes 5, so does $S_n$.
$S_6 = 2.45$: far below 5. The partial sums grow slowly.
That is about the size of a single term, not the partial sum.

items.q: Which statement about the harmonic series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n}$ is true?
options: Its terms approach 0, but its partial sums grow without bound
Its terms approach 0, so it converges to a finite sum
Its partial sums approach $\ln 2$
It diverges because its terms do not approach 0

why.correct: $\frac{1}{n} \to 0$, yet $S_n \ge \ln(n + 1) \to \infty$. The harmonic series diverges, which is why the nth term test can never prove convergence.
options: Right: the standard example that terms approaching 0 do not guarantee convergence.
Terms approaching 0 are necessary for convergence, not enough.
$\ln 2$ is the sum of the alternating harmonic series, not of this one.
Its terms $\frac{1}{n}$ do approach 0; it diverges for another reason.

items.q: Which is true about the alternating harmonic series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} = 1 - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} - \cdots$?
options: It diverges, since $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ diverges
It diverges by the nth term test
It is a $p$-series with $p = 1$, so it diverges
It converges, though $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ diverges

why.correct: The alternating harmonic series is one of the reference series: it converges (its sum is $\ln 2$), while the harmonic series, with the same sizes of terms but all positive, diverges. Topic 10.7 gives the test behind this.
options: The signs matter: positive and negative terms cancel enough for the partial sums to settle.
Its terms approach 0, so the nth term test says nothing.
A $p$-series has positive terms $\frac{1}{n^p}$; the factor $(-1)^{n+1}$ makes this a different series.
Right: the alternating signs make the partial sums settle (to $\ln 2$).
Both converge: the powers are close to 1
Both diverge: the powers are close to 1
The first diverges and the second converges
The first converges and the second diverges

why.correct: A $p$-series converges exactly when $p > 1$: $p = 0.999$ diverges and $p = 1.001$ converges, however close they look.
options: How close $p$ is to 1 does not matter; which side of 1 it is on does.
$p = 1.001 > 1$, so the second converges, slowly.
Reversed: a larger power makes the terms shrink faster, which helps convergence.
No: the numerator 5 is greater than 1
Yes: it is 5 times a $p$-series with $p = 4 > 1$
Yes, to $\frac{5}{4}$
No: it is not a $p$-series

why.correct: $\sum \frac{5}{n^4} = 5\sum \frac{1}{n^4}$, and $\sum \frac{1}{n^4}$ is a $p$-series with $p = 4 > 1$, so the series converges.
options: A constant factor scales the sum; it does not change convergence.
Right: a constant multiple of a convergent series converges.
It converges, but its sum is not $\frac{5}{4}$; the sum of $\sum \frac{1}{n^4}$ is about 1.08.
It is a constant times one: $5\sum \frac{1}{n^4}$.

mistakes.why: Starting at $n = 2$ removes the first term, 1.
That removes the $n = 2$ term. The sum from $n = 2$ keeps it and leaves out $n = 1$.

why.correct: The sum from $n = 2$ leaves out only the first term, $\frac{1}{1^2} = 1$: $\frac{\pi^2}{6} - 1$.

options: Yes: the terms approach 0
Yes: both parts are $p$-series
Yes, to $\frac{\pi^2}{6} - 1$
No: one part diverges and the other converges

why.correct: If $\sum \left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n^2}\right)$ converged, adding the convergent $\sum \frac{1}{n^2}$ would make $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ converge. It does not, so the series diverges.
options: Terms approaching 0 never prove convergence.
Only one part converges; the harmonic part diverges.
That treats $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ as if it had a sum; it diverges.
Right: a convergent series cannot cancel a divergent one.

items.q: For which values of $p$ does $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^p}{n^3}$ converge? Give an interval.

ends.hi: At $p = 2$ the terms are $\frac{1}{n}$: the harmonic series, which diverges, so $p = 2$ is left out.

mistakes.why: Larger $p$ makes the top grow; the power in the denominator is $3 - p$, which must be greater than 1, so $p < 2$.
At $p = 2$ the series is the harmonic series, which diverges.
The power $3 - p$ must be greater than 1, not 0.

why.correct: $\frac{n^p}{n^3} = \frac{1}{n^{3 - p}}$, a $p$-series with power $3 - p$. It converges when $3 - p > 1$, that is $p < 2$.

items.q: The integral test proves the $p$-series result. Find $\int_1^{\infty} x^{-4}\,dx$.

mistakes.why: The antiderivative of $x^{-4}$ is $\frac{x^{-3}}{-3}$; the 3 comes from the new exponent.

items.q: What can be said about $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^2$, the series $\sum \frac{1}{n^p}$ with $p = -2$?
options: It diverges by the nth term test
It converges, since $-2 < 1$
Nothing: it is not a $p$-series
It converges to $\frac{\pi^2}{6}$

why.correct: For $p \le 0$ the terms $\frac{1}{n^p} = n^{-p}$ do not approach 0 (here $n^2 \to \infty$), so the series diverges by the nth term test.
options: Right: $n^2 \to \infty$, so the terms do not approach 0.
$p$-series converge for $p > 1$; with $p = -2$ the terms grow.
It is one with $p = -2$, and the nth term test settles it at once.
That is the sum of $\sum \frac{1}{n^2}$, with $p = 2$, not $p = -2$.
